title: Jurisdiction, Licensing and How to Verify Current Rules

content.overview: Regulatory literacy is the ability to find the rule that actually governs the activity, verify that it is current and preserve enough source information for someone else to reproduce the decision. Cannabis and hemp requirements vary by crop classification, activity and jurisdiction, so a course or search result should never be treated as legal authorization.

vocabulary.definition: The geographic or legal authority under which a rule, license or enforcement program applies.
Formal permission required by an applicable law, regulation, license or regulatory program.
An official statute, regulation, agency rule, license document, product label or authoritative government publication.
The date on which a rule or version becomes operative.
The recorded sequence of official sources used to reach a regulatory conclusion.

sections.title: Define the activity before searching
sections.body: The same location can have different rules for hemp production, non-hemp cannabis, pesticide handling, processing, transport, retail or worker qualifications. Start by writing the exact activity, location and crop/product classification instead of searching broadly for 'cannabis laws.'

sections.title: Identify the controlling authority
sections.body: USDA's hemp framework illustrates why authority must be verified. Depending on location, hemp production may operate under an approved state or tribal plan or direct USDA licensing; approved plans can also change. Non-hemp cannabis authority is separate and must be identified independently.

sections.title: Prefer current primary sources
sections.body: Agency sites, statutes, regulations, license conditions and official program documents are stronger than forum posts, blogs or cached summaries. Record the source URL, version/effective date when available and the date reviewed.

sections.title: Resolve conflicts instead of choosing the convenient answer
sections.body: If an old guide conflicts with a current agency source, or two authorities appear to overlap, do not pick the answer that permits the desired action. Preserve the conflict and escalate to the responsible compliance/legal authority.

sections.title: Education documents competence, not permission
sections.body: THC Academy completion can document that a learner understands a verification process. It does not create a cultivation license, pesticide credential, worker authorization or exemption from employer and jurisdiction requirements.

workedExamples: A grower moves to another state and repeats the verification process instead of assuming the previous license transfers.
A learner sees a search result saying a state has an approved hemp program but checks the current USDA plan list and the state program before acting.
A facility procedure is older than the current agency rule. The discrepancy is documented and escalated instead of silently following the older document.
A proposed activity includes both cultivation and pesticide application. The learner identifies that more than one regulatory authority may apply.
commonMistakes: Searching before defining the exact activity.
Assuming one state's rules apply nationally.
Treating hemp and non-hemp cannabis frameworks as interchangeable.
Using a search snippet as a primary source.
Treating a training certificate as legal authorization.
content.practicalApplication: Build a jurisdiction-verification record for a hypothetical activity. Document location, activity, crop/product classification, controlling authorities, primary sources, source dates/versions, current status, unresolved conflicts and the person/authority to whom uncertainty would be escalated.
content.summary: Regulatory literacy is reproducible source verification. Define the activity, identify the authority, use current primary sources, preserve the source trail and escalate unresolved conflicts.

items.title: Define
items.body: Write the exact location, crop/product classification and activity.

items.title: Identify authority
items.body: Determine which federal, state, tribal, local or facility authority controls each part of the activity.

items.title: Find primary sources
items.body: Use current agency, statute, regulation, license or other official source material.

items.title: Record version and date
items.body: Preserve URL, effective/version date when available and review date.

items.title: Escalate conflicts
items.body: Do not improvise when sources conflict or authorization remains unclear.

blocks.title: Search result vs current program
blocks.setting: A two-year-old article says a state operates under one hemp licensing model. The current USDA page shows a different status.
blocks.prompt: Which source should drive the next verification step?
options: The older article because it explains more
The current USDA status plus the current responsible state/USDA program documents
blocks.answer: The current USDA status plus the current responsible state/USDA program documents.
blocks.feedback: Secondary material can provide context, but current primary program sources should control the verification process.

blocks.title: Build a source trail
prompts: Record the primary source URL and date/version.
Identify what the source proves and what it does not prove.
Record unresolved questions and escalation path.
